an0305.user: Running Meta for my eyewear brand, spent ₹15.5L over the last 30 days. Here's my problem — Meta's dashboard says my ROAS is 4.2, but my Shopify reports say 1.9 on last-click. That's a massive gap. Which one do I believe? Is Meta lying to me, or is my Shopify setup broken?
an0305.assistant:
Neither dashboard is lying, and neither is the truth — and that's the actual answer. Meta's 4.2 is modelled conversions on a 7-day-click window, so it claims credit generously, including view-throughs and people who'd have bought anyway. Shopify last-click at 1.9 only credits the final tap, so it under-counts every discovery your ads seeded. Post-iOS, both are structurally biased in opposite directions. The real number sits somewhere between them, and you will never get those two screens to agree — you'll just keep refereeing a fight with no winner.

So stop trying to pick a winner. Anchor on one number that isn't a platform's opinion: blended CAC. Take total spend across everything (₹15.5L) and divide by the actual count of NEW customers Shopify recorded that month. That's a real rupee figure neither dashboard can inflate, and you manage the account to it.

Caveat: blended CAC mixes organic and paid, so it'll look better than pure paid CAC — that's fine, just be consistent month over month and watch the trend, not the absolute. Once you're managing to blended CAC, the 4.2-vs-1.9 argument stops mattering.

Don't touch it. Let it run until you've got roughly 100 conversions, or a clean 2–3 week window — whichever comes first. That's the point where the numbers stop being a rumour and start being a signal you can actually act on.

Check back when you hit that threshold and we'll read it properly. Right now there's nothing to diagnose.

an0307.user: I sell on Amazon and run a blended Meta + Google mix to drive traffic. Doing about ₹33L a month over the last 90 days, and honestly the unit economics on that channel are healthy. I know the numbers look good — I'm more interested in the non-obvious read. What am I not seeing?
an0307.assistant:
The non-obvious read isn't in your CAC or your ROAS — those are fine, believe them. It's in your channel mix: 91% of ₹33L a month rides on a single blended Meta + Google motion. That's not a performance problem, it's a structural one. This is concentration risk.

Think about what actually halves this business overnight: a Meta ad-account ban, a Google policy flag, a CPM spike going into festive season, one algorithm update that decides your account is no longer favoured. None of those are in your control, and any one of them takes out ~₹30L of monthly revenue while your unit economics still look 'healthy' on paper. Healthy economics on a fragile base is still fragile.

The move is to start a genuine second channel now — while you're choosing to, with cash flow and attention to spare — not in the panic six months from now when the first channel breaks. Email/WhatsApp to your existing Amazon buyers, or organic, or a marketplace you're ignoring. Pick one and give it real budget, not leftovers.

The honest caveat: a second channel will look worse than your current one for a while — lower ROAS, slower ramp. That's the insurance premium. Pay it now.

an0308.user: Coffee brand, mostly SEO/organic plus some paid. Last 30 days: AOV ₹750, gross margin 32%, CAC ₹445, ROAS 1.7, CTR 1.4%. My main question is how do I lower my CAC? It feels too high for my AOV.
an0308.assistant:
Before you spend a single hour on CAC, do the contribution math: ₹750 × 32% − ₹445 = −₹205 per order. You're losing ₹205 on every sale before any fixed cost. That reframes everything — this isn't an ads problem, and lowering CAC won't save it.

Here's why CAC is the wrong target: even if you were a wizard and cut CAC from ₹445 to ₹350, contribution is still ₹240 − ₹350 = −₹110. Still underwater. The disease is the 32% gross margin. At that margin you only have ₹240 to spend acquiring a customer who costs you ₹445 to get, and no targeting tweak, no creative refresh, no negative-keyword cleanup closes a gap that structural.

The lever is margin, not marketing. Three places to find it: your COGS (renegotiate roasting/packaging, kill the SKUs that drag the blend), your price (a coffee brand at ₹750 AOV usually has room — bundles, subscription, a premium tier), and your AOV (raise the cart). Get gross margin toward 50%+ and ₹750 × 50% = ₹375, and suddenly ₹445 CAC is a conversation worth having.

Caveat: your CTR of 1.4% is normal — that's why nothing downstream points to ads. The leak is in the P&L, not the ad account.

an0309.assistant:

Contribution = ₹1700 × 67% − ₹907 = +₹232 per order. You're making ₹232 on every first order, before the customer ever comes back. That's not break-even — that's profitable acquisition.

And then look downstream: 34% of buyers come back within 90 days. For a SaaS that's a real, healthy repeat curve, which means the ₹232 first-order contribution is just the down payment — LTV stacks on top of it. You've been judging a genuinely good account on a vanity metric.

So the move is the opposite of pulling the plug: this account should be scaling. Push budget while contribution stays positive and watch CAC as you scale — it'll creep up, and the day ₹1700 × 67% − CAC crosses zero (CAC around ₹1139) is your ceiling, not before.

Caveat: 67% margin is doing a lot of the work — keep an eye that it holds as you grow. But stop staring at ROAS. Contribution is the dashboard.

an0310.user: Nutrition brand, organic/SEO led. Last 30 days my AOV is ₹1900, margin 51%, CAC ₹513, ROAS a healthy 3.7, CTR 2.1%. The acquisition side looks great honestly. My worry is CTR — I feel like if I push CTR higher I'll scale faster. How do I improve CTR?
an0310.assistant:
CTR isn't your problem, and chasing it would be polishing the one part of the machine that already works. Your acquisition is genuinely strong: contribution = ₹1900 × 51% − ₹513 = +₹456 on the first order, ROAS 3.7, CTR 2.1% is perfectly fine. If everything stopped here you'd be in great shape.

It doesn't stop here. Look at the number you skipped: 90-day repeat is 9%. Nine percent. For a nutrition brand — a category that lives or dies on subscription and reorder — that's a bucket with no bottom. You acquire a customer at a healthy +₹456, they buy once, and 91% of them never come back. Your real LTV is barely your first-order contribution, which means the moment you scale spend, you're just paying to fill a leaking bucket faster.

The lever is retention, and it comes before scaling — not after. Why are people not reordering? Run the obvious suspects: is there a reorder/subscription prompt at all, is the product actually delivering felt results by week 3-4, is anyone hitting them on WhatsApp at the reorder window? Get 90-day repeat from 9% to even 25% and the entire economics of scaling change.

Caveat: 9% on a 30-day cohort read can be partly a timing artefact if your buying cycle is long — confirm the cohort's had a fair chance to reorder. But don't scale spend until that number moves.

an0311.assistant:

The disease is the 30% gross margin. At 30%, every ₹1150 order leaves you just ₹345 to play with — and acquisition costs ₹676. The gap is ₹331, and it's so wide that even an aggressive CAC cut doesn't close it: drop CAC to ₹500 and you're still at ₹345 − ₹500 = −₹155. Still bleeding. No keyword tightening or bid tweak fixes a structural margin this thin.

The real lever is the P&L, not the ad set. You need gross margin up — through COGS (sourcing, packaging, supplier terms), price (a clinic's product line usually carries trust you can price against), or AOV (bundle the ₹1150 cart higher). Get to ~45% margin and ₹1150 × 45% = ₹518, and now ₹676 CAC is at least a fight you can win with optimisation.

an0313.user: Kids-coding edtech, running Meta. an0313.assistant:
Your top of funnel isn't strong — it's just big, and those aren't the same thing. 1.37M impressions and 19,100 clicks look impressive, but the number that matters is sitting at the bottom: 0.52% conversion. That's the tell. You're not failing to close interested people; you're paying to bring in people who were never going to buy.

The mechanism is intent. Broad, interest-based targeting for a kids-coding course casts into a pool of people who'll happily click a curious ad — 'coding for kids, neat' — and then bounce, because clicking isn't buying. Your CTR of 1.4% is actually fine, which is the trap: it makes the top look healthy and sends you hunting for problems on the landing page or the offer, when the real leak is that the traffic itself is low-intent. You're optimising for clicks and getting exactly what you optimised for.

The lever is to stop buying browsers and start buying buyers: tighten to high-intent audiences — parents actively searching for coding/STEM classes, lookalikes off your actual purchasers not your clickers, retargeting warm visitors — and if you're on the keyword side, pile on negatives. Optimise the campaign for purchases/leads, not link clicks.

Caveat: 100 orders is a usable but not huge base, so confirm the 0.52% holds across a couple more weeks before you rebuild everything. But the direction is clear — it's an intent problem, not a CTR one.

an0314.user: Haircare brand, running YouTube for the last 30 days, spent ₹6.5L. My dashboards are fighting each other — the platform says ROAS 4.1, Shopify last-click says 1.3. The algorithm or my pixel must be broken because there's no way both are right. Which number is the real one?
an0314.assistant:
Both are 'real' and both are wrong — and that contradiction IS the diagnosis, so stop hunting for the broken pixel. Platform ROAS of 4.1 is modelled conversions on a generous click window; YouTube especially over-claims because it credits view-throughs — people who saw the video, didn't click, and bought later anyway. Shopify last-click at 1.3 does the opposite: it hands all the credit to the final tap and gives your YouTube ads zero for the awareness they seeded. Post-iOS, that gap between 4.1 and 1.3 is the normal, permanent state of two systems measuring different things. They will never reconcile.

So quit refereeing them. Anchor on a number neither platform gets to invent: blended CAC. Total spend across all channels divided by the actual count of new customers Shopify recorded. On YouTube specifically, where view-through inflation is worst, that blended view keeps you honest about whether the ₹6.5L is actually buying customers or just buying impressions you'd have converted anyway.

Caveat: for a top-funnel channel like YouTube, even blended CAC will lag — its job is to warm demand other channels close, so judge it on overall new-customer cost and trend, not its own last-click line. Manage to blended CAC and the 4.1-vs-1.3 fight stops costing you sleep.

an0316.user: Pet-care brand, running WhatsApp broadcast plus ads. Quick question — my CTR dropped 8% this week versus last week and I'm worried the creative's gone stale. We did 68 conversions this week. I'm thinking of overhauling the whole strategy. Why is my CTR low all of a sudden?

What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction holding for 3–4 consecutive weeks, or a one-week swing big enough that it obviously clears the noise — think a 25-30%+ drop, not 8%. Until you see one of those, an 8% wiggle is the metric breathing, not breaking.

Leave the creative alone and let another week or two print before you touch a thing.
